The induced smoothed lasso works with full $p \times p$ matrices (the derivative of the smoothed
estimating equation and the sandwich covariance matrix), so its cost grows with the number of
covariates. This vignette summarises how **islasso** keeps the computations manageable.

# Cost per iteration

| step | until 1.6.2 | from 1.7.0, $p \le 2n$ | from 1.7.0, $p > 2n$ |
|:-----|:-----------:|:-----------------:|:----------------:|
| estimating equation at fixed s.e. | damped fixed point, one $p\times p$ Cholesky per step | undamped MM (or Newton) steps, one Cholesky per step | $n \times n$ factorisations (Woodbury), $O(n^2p)$ |
| standard errors | full sandwich, $\approx 4.3\,p^3$ flops | diagonal only, $\approx p^3$ flops | diagonal only, $O(n^2p)$ |
| $X^\top W X$ (Gaussian path) | recomputed at every $\lambda$ | computed once | not needed |
| full covariance matrix | every iteration | once, at convergence | once, $O(np^2)$ |

The number of steps needed to solve the estimating equation is also smaller, because the
majorise–minimise iterations are not damped any more (`inner = "mm"`, default) or use Newton's
method (`inner = "newton"`).

# An example with $p \gg n$

```{r}
library(islasso)
n <- 60; p <- 600
beta <- c(2, -2, 1.5, -1.5, 1, rep(0, p - 5))
sim <- simulXy(n = n, p = p, beta = beta, seed = 1, rho = 0.3)
system.time(fit <- islasso(y ~ ., data = sim$data, lambda = 10))
fit$internal$mode   # 1 = Woodbury back end
summary(fit, pval = 0.01)
```

The same model with the dense back end (one $601 \times 601$ factorisation per step):

```{r}
system.time(fit.d <- islasso(y ~ ., data = sim$data, lambda = 10,
                             control = is.control(solver = "dense")))
max(abs(coef(fit) - coef(fit.d)))
```

# Practical advice

* Use `islasso.path()` to explore the tuning parameter: models are fitted with warm starts, from the
  largest to the smallest value of `lambda`, and with the Gaussian family $X^\top W X$ is computed
  once.
* `control = is.control(inner = "newton")` usually needs fewer factorisations when $p$ is large.
* An optimised BLAS/LAPACK library (OpenBLAS, Apple Accelerate, Intel MKL) speeds up all the
  computations, since the numerical core relies on BLAS level 3 and LAPACK routines.
* The full covariance matrix is $p \times p$: with tens of thousands of covariates its storage
  (8 bytes per entry) becomes the limiting factor.
